summary.text: At \(n=7\), the prescribed choice \(x\in\{3,4,6,10,15\}\) forces \(x\ge3\); since \(x\le y\le z\), all three summands are at least \(3\), so their sum is at least \(9\), contradicting \(x+y+z=7\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(a(n)\) denote the number of triples of positive integers
\[
x\le y\le z,\qquad x+y+z=n,
\]
for which all six integers
\[
2x-1,\quad 2y-1,\quad 2z-1,\quad 2xy-1,\quad 2xz-1,\quad 2yz-1
\]
are prime. The conjecture consists of two assertions: first, that \(a(n)>0\) for every \(n>5\); and second, the stronger “moreover” assertion that for every \(n>6\) there is such an ordered triple with
\[
x\in\{3,4,6,10,15\}.
\]
We disprove the combined conjecture by showing that its “moreover” assertion already fails for \(n=7\).

Suppose, for contradiction, that the asserted representation existed for \(n=7\). Then there would be positive integers \(x,y,z\) satisfying
\[
x+y+z=7,\qquad x\le y\le z,
\]
with \(x\in\{3,4,6,10,15\}\), as well as the six stated primality conditions.

Membership in the displayed five-element set gives the finite list of possibilities
\[
x=3,\quad x=4,\quad x=6,\quad x=10,\quad\text{or}\quad x=15.
\]
In every case, \(x\ge 3\). Since the triple is ordered and \(x\le y\le z\), we also have
\[
y\ge x\ge 3\qquad\text{and}\qquad z\ge y\ge x\ge 3.
\]
Consequently,
\[
x+y+z\ge 3+3+3=9.
\]
Equivalently, one may inspect the five possible values of \(x\): they force the sum to be at least \(9,12,18,30,45\), respectively. Each lower bound is strictly greater than \(7\). This contradicts the required equality \(x+y+z=7\).

Thus no positive ordered triple summing to \(7\) can have its least entry \(x\) in \(\{3,4,6,10,15\}\). In particular, no such triple can satisfy all six primality conditions; those conditions need not even be examined, because the elementary size constraints are already inconsistent.

Finally, \(7>6\), so \(n=7\) lies in the claimed range of the “moreover” assertion. Hence that universal assertion is false. Since the stated conjecture includes this assertion as a conjunct, the entire conjecture is false, independently of whether its separate claim \(a(n)>0\) for every \(n>5\) might hold.
